title: Homeland Security’s advice to employees: Don’t talk about work | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

It’s often good advice to avoid talking too much about work at holiday gatherings. Especially, it seems, if you work at the Department of Homeland Security.

Some DHS employees were advised in an email this week to only speak generally about their work with friends and family during the holiday season and were given a list of “appropriate responses” to questions they may receive, according to internal correspondence reviewed by CNN.

The message, sent on behalf of the department’s counterintelligence program division, is titled, “Talking About Your DHS Work with Family and Friends.” It outlines “helpful approaches for holiday conversations” and warns personnel to “be mindful of follow-on questions.”

“If asked, ‘Where do you work?’ you might say: ‘I work for the federal government in the Washington, D.C. area,’” the message advises, reminding employees that “well-meaning family and friends may repeat or share information with others.”

It is common for employees at intelligence agencies and others who deal with sensitive information to avoid being specific about their work, but multiple DHS officials could not recall receiving a holiday message like this in previous years.

The Department of Homeland Security said the reminder to be cautious about sharing classified information was necessary.

“Protecting Homeland Security information requires vigilance both at work and at home, and we are committed to ensuring our employees know the best practices to use outside the office,” an agency spokesperson said in a statement.

The message comes less than a week before Thanksgiving and as the department faces increased scrutiny over multiple controversial actions under the second Trump administration, including ICE-involved shootings of US citizens and immigrants as well as aggressive enforcement tactics. It also comes as DHS has faced scrutiny for its response to potential threats and technological outages that have unnerved Americans.

“DHS is a federal department with a public-facing mission. While it is permissible to speak generally about your public service, it is important to exercise good judgment about what you disclose and toalwayssafeguard classified and controlled unclassified information,” the message says.

Some of the tips included in the correspondence include sharing “general, non-descript information” about work duties, “not confirming, denying, or providing additional details” about work-related information that may have surfaced in the media and “politely redirecting the discussion to personal topics.”

“Whether you support DHS as a federal employee or a contractor, your specific duties are best left out of family gatherings,” it reads.

A portion of the correspondence is also dedicated to mock-up responses to questions that employees may receive.

“If someone continues to press for information or asks questions that make you feel uncomfortable, it is appropriate to calmly restate your boundaries and change the subject,” the email states.

And if the conversation seems “unusual, persistent, threatening, or suspicious,” employees are advised to report it to security or counterintelligence officials at their agencies.

“I’m proud of the work, but I generally keep the details of my job private,” the email suggests as a general response. “How have things been with you?”
